title: How Hoarding Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain hoarding as a recognized mental disorder. They open with banter about recycling pizza boxes, glass recycling, and old malt liquor brands, then announce that Caroline Irvin and Kristen Conger have launched a new podcast, Unladylike. The main discussion covers the early 1990s research by David Frost, Rachel Gross and Tamara Hardel, and the 2013 DSM-5 listing. They describe symptoms (acquiring, inability to discard, disorganization, shame, impaired living space, debt), myths (laziness, Depression-era upbringing, older-people-only, OCD equivalence, cleaning out cures it), possible causes and brain research, evolutionary gathering theories, the Collyer brothers case, animal hoarding, and treatment through cognitive behavioral talk therapy with family support. The episode closes with a listener mail and sign-off.

entities.name: Anxiety and Depression Association of America

segments.title: Opening banter and pizza box recycling
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about pizza box recycling, glass recycling in Atlanta, and past cheap malt liquor and bottle brands before moving on.

segments.title: Unladylike podcast announcement
segments.summary: The hosts announce that former Stuff Mom Never Told You hosts Caroline Irvin and Kristen Conger have launched a new podcast called Unladylike.

segments.title: Introduction to hoarding and its research history
segments.summary: Hoarding is introduced as a known cultural phenomenon. Early research by David Frost and students Rachel Gross and Tamara Hardel led to its recognition as a disorder and its inclusion in the DSM-5 in 2013.

segments.title: Prevalence and age of onset
segments.summary: Estimates of prevalence range from 0.4 to 5 percent of people. Hoarding is often thought to affect only older people because it is progressive and is only noticed late, but it typically starts much earlier in life.

segments.title: Hoarding versus family members' clutter and sentimental attachment
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish ordinary difficulty discarding things from hoarding, citing relatives who keep stuff and a grandfather who saved rusty nails. They note that sentiment and stockpiling rationalizations are typical hoarder reasoning.

segments.title: Symptoms of hoarding
segments.summary: Symptoms include an inability to get rid of things and to stop acquiring them, including unworn clothing with tags. Hoarders also feel shame, and disorganization is a key marker. The hosts discuss whether being organized rules out hoarding. The condition also impairs living space, causes goat paths, disrepair, and debt.

segments.title: Myths about hoarding
segments.summary: Myths covered include that hoarding affects only older people, that hoarders are lazy, that it stems from Depression-era scarcity, and that it is just OCD. Freud's view on harsh toilet training is mentioned. Cleaning out a home does not cure hoarding, and relapse is likely without treatment.

segments.title: Causes and brain research on hoarding
segments.summary: The cause is unknown. Candidate factors include brain lesions, chromosomal defects, genetics, and trauma such as loss of a loved one or harsh discipline. Brain studies found stress responses when discarding possessions. An evolutionary theory of gathering is also discussed.

segments.title: Collyer brothers case
segments.summary: Homer and Langley Collyer are described. Langley hoarded and was crushed by his stuff, and Homer, who was blind, starved to death in their Harlem brownstone. The case was covered in an earlier episode and a park was named after them.

segments.title: Animal hoarding
segments.summary: Animal hoarding is described as a sad form of hoarding in which owners with good intentions accumulate animals who suffer from crowding, disease and neglect. Statistics are given on authority cases and on the demographics of animal hoarders, many of whom are single, widowed, or divorced women.

segments.title: Treatment and family support
segments.summary: Treatment is mainly cognitive behavioral talk therapy, which challenges beliefs about discarding. Gradual progress is needed, family support matters, and hoarders without family are most at risk. The hosts close by suggesting kindness toward hoarders.

segments.title: Listener mail on Christmas music and oven windows
segments.summary: A listener writes about listening to Christmas music in December and laughing at the hosts' conversation about oven doors. The hosts respond briefly and give social media and website contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck sign off and thank listeners for contacting them.
